content: Malaria is an infectious disease caused by a parasite. The parasite is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected mosquitoes. Symptoms of malaria typically manifest within 7 to 30 days after being bitten, but in some cases, they may take up to a year to appear. Common symptoms include high fever, shaking chills, and flu-like illness. If left untreated, malaria can lead to severe complications and even death. The mosquitoes responsible for spreading malaria are predominantly found in regions such as Africa, Central and South America, parts of the Caribbean, Asia, Eastern Europe, and the South Pacific. Travelers visiting these areas are at risk of being bitten by infected mosquitoes and contracting the disease. Approximately 2,000 cases of malaria are diagnosed annually in the United States, primarily among individuals who have recently returned from travel to these regions. Currently, there is no vaccine available for malaria. It is essential to consult a healthcare provider to determine the appropriate antimalarial medication based on the travel destination. Some medications need to be started several days before travel and continued during and after the trip. To prevent mosquito bites, travelers should use insect repellents registered with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). These repellents should contain active ingredients such as picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE), or para-menthane-diol (PMD). When applying both sunscreen and insect repellent, the repellent should be applied after the sunscreen. Pregnant and breastfeeding women can safely use EPA-registered repellents when used as directed. For children, additional precautions should be taken, such as dressing them in clothing that covers their arms and legs, using mosquito netting over strollers, and avoiding the application of repellents containing OLE or PMD on children under three years old. Repellent should not be applied to a child’s hands, eyes, mouth, or irritated skin. Adults should spray repellent onto their hands before applying it to a child’s face. Clothing and gear can be treated with 0.5% permethrin, an insecticide that repels and kills mosquitoes and other insects. Permethrin-treated clothing remains effective after multiple washes, but it is important to follow product instructions for proper use. Permethrin should never be applied directly to the skin. If these are not available, or if sleeping outdoors, using a mosquito net is recommended. Mosquito nets should be compact, white, rectangular, and have 156 holes per square inch. They should be long enough to tuck under the mattress for full protection. Permethrin-treated mosquito nets offer enhanced protection compared to untreated nets. Always follow label instructions to determine if treated nets can be washed. If bitten by mosquitoes, avoid scratching the bites to prevent secondary infections. Over-the-counter anti-itch creams or antihistamines can be applied to alleviate itching. For more information on managing mosquito bites, refer to resources on symptoms and treatment.
